question: The 6th Global Conference on the Elimination of Child Labour acknowledged that Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) target 8.7 of eliminating child labour by 2025 has not been achieved. An estimated 138 million children remain in child labour and progress would need to accelerate elevenfold to meet global commitments.

The revised EU Guidelines on Children and Armed Conflict also note that 470 million children live in conflict-affected settings, where forced recruitment, sexual exploitation and hazardous labour remain widespread. 1.

Which indicators, benchmarks and monitoring mechanisms in the Marrakech Global Framework for Action does the Commission intend to use to assess the contribution of the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) and the Forced Labour Regulation (FLR) towards achieving SDG target 8.7?

Pending the full application of the FLR and the CSDDD, how does the Commission intend to address the interim accountability gap, and what transitional oversight, reporting or enforcement measures will be put in place to ensure continued scrutiny of child labour risks in global supply chains, including the meaningful participation of civil society organisations and child labour survivors?

How does the Commission intend to assess and report on the progress of its Member States and trade partners in eliminating child labour, while ensuring transparency and accountability in measuring progress?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.8.2026) The Commission is deeply committed to the eradication of child labour, in particular its worst forms, and to promoting and protecting children’s rights in line with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child1, the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union2, and the International Labour Organization (ILO) Fundamental Conventions3.

To this end, the Commission supports the universal ratification and effective implementation of all ILO Fundamental Conventions, including No 138 on the Minimum Age and No 182 on the Worst Forms of Child Labour.

The Commission welcomes the ILO’s monitoring of global and national progress, including through its global estimates, country-level reporting and analytical work, drawing on the indicators from the Annex to the Marrakech Global Framework for Action4.

As provided for in the respective legal instruments, the Commission will evaluate and report to the European Parliament and Council on the implementation and effectiveness of both the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive5 and the Forced Labour Regulation6, including in preventing and addressing adverse impacts related to child labour.

Pending their entry into application, the Commission will continue to promote responsible business conduct through existing policies, engage with partner countries and international organisations, civil society, trade unions and affected communities and support multistakeholder initiatives to contribute to the eradication of child labour.

The Commission is also working on a new EU Strategy on Combatting Trafficking in Human Beings, which also intends to address child labour. Progress in partner countries will continue to be monitored through cooperation with the ILO, relevant UN agencies and other international partners.
1 Convention on the Rights of the Child, Adopted and opened for signature, ratification and accession by General

Assembly resolution 44/25 of 20 November 1989, entry into force 2 September 1990. 2 Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, 2012/C 326/02. 3 ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work (1998), as amended in 2022. https://normlex.ilo.org/dyn/nrmlx_en/f?p=1000:62:0::NO:62:P62_LIST_ENTRIE_ID:2453911:NO. 4 https://www.ilo.

org/publications/marrakech-global-framework-action-against-child-labour. 5 Directive (EU) 2024/1760 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 on corporate sustainability due diligence and amending Directive (EU) 2019/1937 and Regulation (EU) 2023/2859.

6 Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2024 on prohibiting products made with forced labour on the Union market and amending Directive (EU) 2019/1937.
